questions.prompt: Which of these is listed as an advantage of a microservice architecture?

options.text: The application is simpler to develop overall
Cross-service transactions become trivial
Services can be deployed independently
Service discovery becomes unnecessary

questions.explanation: Independent deployability (and independent scalability) is a core μS advantage. Monoliths are actually simpler to develop/deploy/scale as a unit; cross-service transactions get harder (sagas); and RPC-based μS need service discovery.

questions.prompt: Select the drawbacks of microservices highlighted in the slides.

options.text: Finding the right set of services is hard
Distributed systems add development complexity
Features spanning services need coordination
Code duplication is automatically eliminated
Fault isolation becomes impossible

questions.explanation: Drawbacks: hard to find the right service boundaries, distributed-system complexity, and coordinating features that span services. μS actually improve fault isolation, and they do not magically remove duplication.

questions.prompt: Decomposition by business capability groups services around…

options.text: how the code is currently structured
what the organization does (not how)
the shared relational database schema
the screens exposed by the user interface

questions.explanation: A business capability is what an organization does, as opposed to how. It is derived from the organization structure and yields cohesive, loosely coupled services.

questions.prompt: "Classes that change for the same reason should be in the same package" states the…

options.text: Single Responsibility Principle
Dependency Inversion Principle
Common Closure Principle
Interface Segregation Principle

questions.explanation: The Common Closure Principle: classes that change for the same reason belong together. The slides pair it with the Single Responsibility Principle when decomposing by business capability.

questions.prompt: In DDD, two value objects with identical values are considered interchangeable.
questions.explanation: True. A value object represents a collection of values; two with the same values are interchangeable. An entity, by contrast, has a persistent identity, so equal values still mean distinct items.

questions.prompt: What distinguishes an Entity from a Value Object in DDD?

options.text: An Entity is always immutable once created
An Entity cannot be stored in a database
An Entity is interchangeable when values match
An Entity has a persistent identity

questions.explanation: An entity has a persistent identity, so two entities with the same field values are still different items. Value objects are the interchangeable-by-value ones. Entities are typically persisted to a DB.

questions.prompt: Which DDD class pattern holds business logic that does not belong to a single entity?

options.text: Repository
Factory
Service
Value object

questions.explanation: A Service implements business logic that doesn't fit a single entity. Factory builds objects (hiding the concrete class); Repository provides access to persistent entities; Value object holds values.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the Repository pattern?

options.text: Construct objects while hiding the concrete class
Provide access to persistent entities
Hold business logic spanning several entities
Represent an immutable collection of values

questions.explanation: A Repository provides access to persistent entities and hides DB access. Constructing objects is the Factory's job; cross-entity logic is a Service; a collection of values is a Value object.

questions.prompt: The "reference roots only" aggregate rule requires that…

options.text: external code references only the root
every internal object exposes a public setter
aggregates reference each other by pointer
each field is loaded with a separate query

questions.explanation: Only the aggregate root may be referenced from outside, and updates go through the root's methods. This lets the aggregate enforce invariants and serialize its updates.

questions.prompt: How should one aggregate reference another aggregate?

options.text: Through a direct in-memory object reference
By the other aggregate's primary key
Via a shared foreign-key join table
With a mutable pointer shared across services

questions.explanation: Inter-aggregate references must use primary keys, not object references (object references between aggregates are a code smell). This keeps aggregates loosely coupled and lets them live in distinct services.

questions.prompt: A consequence of the "one aggregate per transaction" rule is that…

options.text: a transaction stays within a single service
every request updates many aggregates at once
transactions require a two-phase commit
the database must support full ACID isolation

questions.explanation: If a transaction touches only one aggregate, it stays inside one service — which suits the limited transaction support of many NoSQL databases. Multi-aggregate requests become harder, handled via sagas.

questions.prompt: Which are benefits of FINE-grained aggregates?

options.text: Better scalability since updates are serialized
Lower risk of update conflicts
Easier decomposition into services
All related entities fit in one transaction
Simpler handling of multi-aggregate requests

questions.explanation: Fine-grained aggregates improve scalability (serialized updates), reduce conflict risk, and decompose into services more easily. Fitting many entities in one transaction and simpler multi-aggregate requests are coarse-grained advantages.

questions.prompt: How is a domain event name conventionally formed?

options.text: As an imperative command verb
As a past-participle verb
As a present-continuous verb
As a noun with no verb at all

questions.explanation: Domain events are named with a past-participle verb (e.g. OrderCreated) because they describe something that already happened. They also carry metadata such as event ID and timestamp.

questions.prompt: Which is a drawback of synchronous RPC noted in the slides?

options.text: It cannot support the simple request/reply style
Reduced availability: both ends must be up
It always requires a message broker
It is unfamiliar to most developers

questions.explanation: RPC reduces availability because client and service must both be up for the whole interaction. RPC is simple/familiar, needs no broker, and does request/reply well — but struggles with notifications and pub/sub.

questions.prompt: How does the Circuit Breaker pattern behave?

options.text: It retries the failing call immediately and forever
It fails fast once errors pass a threshold
It queues requests until the service recovers
It load-balances calls across healthy nodes

questions.explanation: When the error rate crosses a threshold the breaker trips and further calls fail immediately (fail fast). After a timeout it lets a trial call through and, if it succeeds, closes again (Hystrix, Polly).

questions.prompt: In the client-side discovery pattern, who selects the service instance?

options.text: The client queries the registry and load-balances
A platform-side router resolves the address through DNS
The service registrar selects it on startup
A third-party broker assigns the instance

questions.explanation: Client-side discovery (application level): the client queries the registry for live instances and applies its own load-balancing. Server-side discovery (platform level) hides this behind a router/DNS.

questions.prompt: Message brokers usually guarantee at-least-once delivery, so a message may be delivered more than once.
questions.explanation: True. Delivery is guaranteed at least once but not exactly once, so duplicates can occur. Countermeasures include idempotent messages and message tracking.

questions.prompt: How does the transactional outbox keep data and messaging consistent?

options.text: It commits the message to the broker before the DB write
It queues the message in the same DB transaction
It uses a distributed two-phase commit
It polls every service for state changes

questions.explanation: Transactional messaging uses a DB table as a queue, so the application update and the message enqueue commit in one local transaction — avoiding the dual-write problem without a distributed transaction.

questions.prompt: "Database per service" means that…

options.text: all services share one schema and DB
a service's data is private to its API
every service uses the same DB server
services read each other's tables directly

questions.explanation: Each service's persistent data is private and reachable only via its API (private tables, schema, or DB server per service). A service's transactions involve only its own database.

questions.prompt: What is a saga?

options.text: A single distributed ACID transaction spanning all services
A sequence of local transactions coordinated by messages
A two-phase commit shared by all services
A global lock held for the whole flow

questions.explanation: A saga is a sequence of local transactions; each updates its DB and emits a message/event triggering the next. On failure it runs compensating transactions to undo prior steps — an alternative to 2PC.

questions.prompt: In a saga, the "pivot" transaction is…

options.text: the first compensatable step
the go/no-go point of the saga
any step guaranteed to be retriable
the compensating step run on failure

questions.explanation: The pivot is the go/no-go point: once it succeeds the saga can run to completion. Steps before it are compensatable (can be rolled back); steps after it are retriable (guaranteed to succeed).

questions.prompt: Which of these are saga countermeasures for the lack of isolation?

options.text: Semantic lock
Commutative updates
Two-phase commit across services
Reread value
Global serializable isolation

questions.explanation: Countermeasures include semantic lock, commutative updates, reread value (plus pessimistic view, version file, by value). Two-phase commit and a global serializable level are exactly what sagas avoid.

questions.prompt: How does event sourcing persist an aggregate?

options.text: As one current-state row via an ORM
As a sequence of state-change events
As a JSON snapshot replaced each update
As a cached copy in the API gateway

questions.explanation: Event sourcing stores the aggregate as the series of events that changed it; current state is rebuilt by replaying them. It reliably publishes events and preserves history, but querying the event store is harder.

questions.prompt: How does CQRS make cross-service queries easy?

options.text: It shards the write database by tenant
It keeps a read-only view fed by events
It caches every query inside the client
It runs the queries on the message broker

questions.explanation: CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation) uses events to maintain a read-only view that replicates data from services, designed to match the queries — at the cost of coping with replication lag.

questions.prompt: The API Composition pattern answers a composed query by…

options.text: joining tables across all of the service databases
calling each service API and merging results
replicating all data into one big database
asking the client to call each service

questions.explanation: An API Composer queries each provider service via its API and combines the results (parallelizing where possible). The composer may be a client, an API gateway, or a standalone service.

questions.prompt: Which approach migrates a monolith to microservices incrementally?

options.text: A big-bang full rewrite
Strangling the monolith
A one-shot lift and shift
Freezing the monolith permanently

questions.explanation: The Strangler pattern grows a new system around the edges of the old one until the monolith is strangled. Big-bang rewrites are risky — "the only thing a Big Bang rewrite guarantees is a Big Bang!" (Fowler).

questions.prompt: Decomposition by subdomain identifies services based on…

options.text: bounded contexts / DDD sub-domains that partition the overall domain model
the existing relational tables
the screens of the user interface
the programming language used

questions.explanation: Decomposing by subdomain identifies bounded contexts (DDD sub-domains) that partition the overall domain model, yielding cohesive, loosely coupled services and a stable architecture for autonomous teams.

questions.prompt: Which are listed as obstacles to decomposition?

options.text: Network latency
Reduced availability due to synchronous communication
Data consistency across services and god classes
Automatic removal of all coupling

questions.explanation: Decomposition obstacles include network latency, reduced availability from synchronous communication, data consistency across services, getting a consistent view of data, and god classes.

questions.prompt: When is the Transaction Script pattern appropriate, and what is its downside?

options.text: For simple business logic (a sequence of steps); downside is code duplication and being hard to maintain
For complex logic; downside is no code duplication
For querying multiple services; downside is replication lag
For event-sourced aggregates; downside is a learning curve

questions.explanation: Transaction Script suits simple business logic organised as procedures (one service class method per request); all code for a request is in one place but it causes duplication and is hard to maintain/refactor.

questions.prompt: What characterizes the Domain Model pattern for business logic?

options.text: Complex logic in OO classes encapsulating code and data (DDD); no duplication, easy to maintain and extend
A single procedure per request with duplicated code
Storing aggregates only as event sequences
A read-only view fed by events

questions.explanation: The Domain Model suits complex logic: OO classes encapsulate both code and data (DDD); code is spread across classes with no duplication, easy to maintain, refactor, and extend (e.g. with Strategy or Template Method).

questions.prompt: In the Ports & Adapters (hexagonal) architecture, how is the business logic structured?

options.text: A core business logic accessed through inbound and outbound adapters via ports
A single layered stack with the database on top
A pipeline of stateless filters
A god class controlling all other objects

questions.explanation: Ports & Adapters puts business logic at the core, reachable through inbound adapters (e.g. web) and outbound adapters (e.g. DB, web services) via in/out ports — separating domain from infrastructure.

questions.prompt: What is the role of the DDD Factory pattern?

options.text: Implement object construction, possibly hiding the concrete class
Provide access to persistent entities
Hold business logic spanning several entities
Represent an interchangeable collection of values

questions.explanation: A Factory implements object construction and may hide the concrete class; Repository accesses persistent entities, Service holds cross-entity logic, and a Value object holds values.

questions.prompt: What is an aggregate in the Aggregate pattern?

options.text: A graph of objects that can be treated as a unit, self-contained and sharing the same life cycle
A single database table
A read-only projection of events
A network proxy for remote calls

questions.explanation: An aggregate organises the domain model as a graph of objects treated as a unit — self-contained chunks that clarify operation scope, where all elements share the same life cycle.

questions.prompt: What is an advantage of COARSE-grained aggregates?

options.text: They are more suitable for fitting all relevant entities into a single transaction
They maximize scalability through serialized updates
They minimize the risk of update conflicts
They make decomposition into services easier

questions.explanation: Coarse-grained aggregates fit more relevant entities into one transaction; fine-grained aggregates instead favour scalability, fewer conflicts, and easier service decomposition.

questions.prompt: Which are stated uses of domain events?

options.text: Maintaining data consistency across services
Notifying a service that maintains a replica that source data changed
Notifying another application via a webhook or message broker
Replacing the need for any database

questions.explanation: Domain events maintain cross-service consistency, notify replicas, send user notifications, trigger related updates, notify other apps via webhook/broker, and support monitoring and behaviour analysis.

questions.prompt: What does API-first design recommend to avoid late integration issues?

options.text: Define the interface (with an IDL), review with client developers, iterate to consensus, then implement
Implement the service first and document it afterwards
Skip interface definition and rely on runtime discovery
Let each client invent its own contract

questions.explanation: API-first design ensures agreement on the interaction mechanism: define the interface with an IDL, review with client-service developers, iterate to consensus, then start implementing.

questions.prompt: What does the 'robustness principle' for API evolution state?

options.text: Be conservative in what you do, be liberal in what you accept from others
Break compatibility freely as long as you document it
Never accept unexpected input
Always require clients to upgrade simultaneously

questions.explanation: API evolution aims for minor backward-compatible changes following the robustness principle: be conservative in what you do, liberal in what you accept from others (cf. Lehman's first law).

questions.prompt: Which are binary message formats mentioned for inter-service communication?

options.text: Protocol Buffers (used by gRPC)
Avro
JSON
XML

questions.explanation: Binary formats include Protocol Buffers (gRPC) and Avro; JSON and XML are the text-based formats. The format may be mandated by the communication mechanism.

questions.prompt: Which techniques make synchronous APIs robust?

options.text: Network timeouts (never block indefinitely)
Limiting the number of outstanding requests
The circuit breaker pattern (fail fast)
Removing service discovery

questions.explanation: Robust synchronous APIs use network timeouts, an upper bound on outstanding requests per service, and the circuit breaker pattern to fail fast.

questions.prompt: Why is service discovery needed in an RPC-based microservices system?

options.text: Service instances change continuously due to autoscaling, failures, and upgrades
Because messages are always asynchronous
Because databases are shared between services
Because the monolith never changes location

questions.explanation: With RPC you need a service's network location, but instances change continuously due to autoscaling, failures, and upgrades — hence service discovery.

questions.prompt: In the third-party / server-side (platform-level) discovery pattern, who performs registration and resolution?

options.text: A registrar component (often part of the platform, e.g. Docker/Kubernetes) registers instances, and a router resolves DNS requests via the registry
The client queries the registry and load-balances itself
Each service hard-codes the addresses of the others
No registry is involved at all

questions.explanation: In platform-level discovery a registrar (often Docker/Kubernetes) registers instances, and in server-side discovery the client makes a DNS request that a router resolves via the registry with load balancing.

questions.prompt: How do sharded (partitioned) channels handle competing receivers needing ordered, once-only processing?

options.text: The sender puts a shard key in the message header and the broker assigns the message to a partition
Every receiver processes every message independently
The broker randomly drops duplicate messages
Messages are broadcast to all shards at once

questions.explanation: With sharded channels the sender specifies a shard key in the message header; the broker uses it to assign the message to a particular shard/partition, so each message is processed once and in order.

questions.prompt: Which are stated limits of distributed (2PC) transactions?

options.text: Not universally supported (e.g. NoSQL DBs, modern message brokers)
Synchronous, which reduces availability
You cannot have both availability and the most recent data
They guarantee perfect isolation for free

questions.explanation: Distributed transactions aren't universally supported (NoSQL, brokers), are synchronous (reducing availability), and can't provide both availability and most-recent data; isolation is also 'overrated' as most DBs use weaker levels.

questions.prompt: Sagas provide ACD but not isolation. What does that imply?

options.text: They are Atomic, Consistent, and Durable, but non-isolated, so anomalies like dirty reads can occur
They give full ACID guarantees automatically
They are isolated but not durable
They cannot be rolled back at all

questions.explanation: Sagas are Atomic (via coordination/compensation), Consistent (each service locally), and Durable (local DBs), but non-isolated — so lost updates, dirty reads, and non-repeatable reads can occur.

questions.prompt: What is a 'retriable' transaction in a saga?

options.text: One that follows the pivot transaction and is guaranteed to succeed
One that can be rolled back with a compensating transaction
The go/no-go point of the saga
A transaction that always fails first

questions.explanation: Retriable transactions follow the pivot and are guaranteed to succeed; compensatable transactions precede the pivot and can be rolled back; the pivot is the go/no-go point.

questions.prompt: How does the 'semantic lock' countermeasure work?

options.text: A compensatable transaction sets a flag on records it creates/updates to signal they are not fully committed
It acquires a global database lock for the whole saga
It reorders saga steps to reduce risk
It records operations so they can be reordered

questions.explanation: A semantic lock is an application-level lock: a compensatable transaction flags records as not fully committed; the flag is cleared by a retriable transaction (success) or a compensating transaction (rollback).

questions.prompt: Which are advantages of event sourcing?

options.text: Reliably publishes domain events
Preserves the history of aggregates (a 'time machine')
Avoids the object/relational impedance mismatch
Makes querying the event store trivial

questions.explanation: Event sourcing reliably publishes domain events, preserves aggregate history (a time machine), and avoids the O/R impedance mismatch; querying the event store, however, is challenging.

questions.prompt: Which patterns address the problems of exposing services to external clients?

options.text: API Gateway and Backend-for-Frontend
Saga and CQRS
Circuit Breaker and Bulkhead
Transaction Script and Domain Model

questions.explanation: External clients face low bandwidth, lack of encapsulation, and differing communication mechanisms; solutions are the API Gateway and Backend-for-Frontend patterns.

questions.prompt: Which responsibilities are handled by edge functions (e.g. in an API gateway)?

options.text: Authentication and authorization
Rate limiting and caching
Metrics collection and request logging
Compiling the service source code

questions.explanation: Edge functions cover authentication, authorization, rate limiting, caching, metrics collection, and request logging.

questions.prompt: Which are strategies for transitioning a monolith to microservices?

options.text: Implement new features as services (stop the monolith's growth)
Separate presentation from backend (intermediate strategy)
Break up the monolith by extracting functionalities into services
Perform a big-bang rewrite

questions.explanation: Transition strategies: implement new features as services, separate presentation and backend, and break up the monolith by extracting functionalities; big-bang rewrites are discouraged.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended way to split a 'God Class' such as Order?

options.text: Apply DDD: separate the domain model into subdomains, each with its own possibly partial model, avoiding a shared library/central DB
Wrap it in a single shared library used by all services
Turn it into one central data service for everyone
Leave it as is since most apps have one

questions.explanation: Splitting a God Class via DDD separates the domain into subdomains with their own partial models, avoiding the tight coupling of a shared library/central DB or a data service; different Order views are kept consistent with sagas and adapted via an API gateway.
